title: Barley, deer and desire
hookLine: the book lets its critics speak first
carry: kama is a true aim, kept within dharma
tomorrow: the critics come back: a pigeon now, or a peacock later?

lines: A BAD REVIEW IN THE WINDOW.
A BOOK ON PLEASURE, AGAINST PLEASURE.
cards: Now and then a café tapes its harshest review to the front window, right where you'd see it walking in. Odd marketing. Odder still is what the Kama Sutra does in its opening chapters.

A book on pleasure stops to make the case against pleasure. Some people, it says, hold that kama shouldn't be pursued at all: it gets in the way of dharma and of wealth, and makes people careless and easy to lead astray.

The text even names those whose desire brought them down: Indra, punished for deceiving Ahalya; Kichaka, killed for pursuing Draupadi; Ravana, ruined for seizing Sita. Then it lets that case stand. So who wins?

teach.b: Vatsyayana answers in three short moves. Pleasures are needed for the body's life and health, the way food is. They come as the fruit of dharma and wealth, not as their enemy.
And, the part that's easy to skip, they're to be followed with moderation and caution. Then come two pictures from daily life.
Nobody stops cooking because a beggar might come to the door asking for the food. Nobody stops sowing barley because deer might come and eat the crop. That solves the puzzle of the window.
He doesn't say Ravana was fine, or that the danger is made up. The deer are real.

teach.h: A RISK DOESN'T CANCEL A NEED.
teach.b: His point is narrower: a risk doesn't cancel a need. You plant anyway, and you keep watch. So neither side wins outright.

teach.h: SOMETHING IN BETWEEN, HELD WITH CARE.
teach.b: Not give it all up, and not take everything you want, but something in between, held with care. That is the classic Hindu place for desire.
In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says that in all beings he is desire that does not go against dharma.
Kama is a real aim of life, not a sin to stamp out, as long as dharma holds it. So when a family feasts and dances at a wedding or a festival, that isn't a lapse from the faith.
It's one of the faith's own aims, kept in its place.

how: Students of the Kama Sutra often point to its opening as a set piece of argument: an objection stated fully, then answered.

games.q: what does “the kama sutra's ethics chapter” mean?
o: a book that tells readers to give up every pleasure
a book that tells readers pleasure has no risks
an old opening that weighs pleasure against its critics

games.q: the critics and the answer — tap the pairs.

s: the Kama Sutra simply tells readers to take all the pleasure they can
its answer to the critics ends with moderation and caution.
the book states its critics' case before answering it
it names those whose desire ruined them, like Ravana, who seized Sita.
Vatsyayana says the critics' warnings are made up
he never says the danger is false; he says kama is still a true aim, kept with moderation and caution.

games.q: at a cousin's wedding, a friend leans over: 'i thought hinduism was all about giving things up. why is everyone feasting and dancing?' what's the Kama Sutra's answer?
o: pleasure is one of life's real aims, enjoyed within dharma.
hindus secretly think it's wrong; a wedding is just a day off.
pleasure is the top aim, so anything goes at a wedding.
games.why: Vatsyayana answers pleasure's critics: needed like food, the fruit of dharma and wealth, kept with moderation. in the Gita, Krishna calls himself desire that doesn't go against dharma.

practice: Before your next meal or snack, do what many Hindu families do at the table: offer it first, silently, to God, the way food becomes prasad. If you don't pray, pause and give thanks instead. Then eat, and enjoy it fully.
Pleasure, offered first, and kept inside dharma.

wordCard.voice: The Kama Sutra's ethics chapter: here, pleasure defended against its critics, and kept with moderation and caution.

orig.note: Sanskrit kamasutra, the name of Vatsyayana's book; kama is pleasure and love, one of the three aims of life.

carryVoice: Your line: kama is a true aim, kept within dharma. Plant the barley, and watch for deer. That's fifteen ninety-eight.

sources.ref: Kama Sutra 1.2 (the objection that kama should not be pursued; examples of those ruined by desire, incl. Indra and Ahalya, Kichaka and Draupadi, Ravana and Sita; Vatsyayana's answer: needed like food, the fruit of dharma and artha, to be followed with moderation and caution; the cooking and barley sayings)
Bhagavad Gita 7.11 (Krishna: in beings I am desire not opposed to dharma)
